listeningParts.title: Enrolling on an evening course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a community college to enrol on an evening language course.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Community College, Enrolment Office. Lucy speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'd like some information about your evening language courses, please. I'm hoping to start one this autumn.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Certainly. Which language were you interested in?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Spanish. My company is opening an office in Mexico next year, and I might be working there for a few months.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Lovely. And have you studied Spanish before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A little, at school, but that was a long time ago. I can remember some basic phrases, but that's about it.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Then you'd probably want our Spanish Level Two course, which is for people who've had some contact with the language but aren't confident. If you're not sure, you can do a short placement test online before you enrol. It only takes about twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll do that, thanks. When does the course run?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Level Two runs on Tuesday evenings, from seven until nine. There used to be a Thursday group as well, but we've had to cancel that this year because the tutor has moved away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Tuesday is fine. How long is the course?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: It's thirty weeks, starting on the twenty-third of September, with breaks at Christmas and Easter, and it finishes in June.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And the cost?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: The full fee is three hundred and forty pounds for the year. That includes the course book, but not the online exercises, which are optional and cost an extra twenty pounds. If you're a student, over sixty, or receiving certain benefits, you can get a concession, which brings the fee down to one hundred and ninety.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm afraid I don't qualify for any of those. Can I pay in instalments?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Yes, you can pay in three instalments: one when you enrol, one in January and one in April.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That would help. What's the class size?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: The maximum is sixteen, but most groups have around twelve. The tutor for Level Two is Carmen Ortega, who's from Madrid. She's been teaching here for about ten years and she's very popular.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And where are the classes held?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Not in the main building, I'm afraid. Evening language classes are in the Elm Building, which is just across the car park. It's the one with the blue door. Parking is free after six.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there somewhere to get a coffee before class? I'll be coming straight from work.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: The main café closes at five, but there's a vending machine in the Elm Building, and the student common room on the ground floor stays open until nine. Lots of evening students eat there before their class.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Is there anything I need to bring to the first class?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Just a notebook and a pen. You'll get the book at the first lesson. Oh, and Carmen likes everyone to bring a photo of somewhere they've visited, because the first lesson is about travel and introducing yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fun. I'll find one from my last holiday. Is there an exam at the end?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: There's no compulsory exam. But if you want a qualification, you can take an optional assessment in May, and if you pass, you get a certificate from the college. Many people find it useful for their job.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That could be useful for me. How do I enrol?

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: You can do it online or I can take your details now. Can I have your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Graham Fairweather.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Could you spell the surname?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: F-A-I-R-W-E-A-T-H-E-R.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And an email address?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's g dot fairweather at mailbox dot com.

dialogue.speaker: Administrator
dialogue.text: Lovely. I'll send you the link to the placement test and a confirmation. If the test shows you should be in a different level, we'll move you, so don't worry.

listeningParts.title: A guided walk through the botanical garden
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a botanical garden and explains its history and layout.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Morning, everyone. Welcome to the Halton Botanical Garden. I'm Josh, and I'll be showing you around this morning. Before we start walking, let me give you a bit of background and point out where things are, because the garden is bigger than it looks from the gate.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The garden was founded in 1820 by the university, originally as a place to grow plants for medical students to study. Back then, most medicines came from plants, so future doctors had to be able to recognise them. Today, our main work is conservation. We grow over twelve thousand species, and around four hundred of them are threatened in the wild.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, if you look at the map on the board here, we're at the main gate, at the bottom. The path in front of us leads straight up the middle of the garden to the lake. On your left as you walk up, the first area you come to is the herb garden, which is the oldest part of the site and still laid out in the original pattern from the 1820s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Opposite the herb garden, on the right of the main path, is the rock garden, where we grow alpine plants from mountain regions around the world. It's at its best in late spring, so you've come at a good time.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Carry on up the main path and you'll reach the lake. The glasshouses are on the far side of the lake, at the very top of the map. There are three of them: one for tropical plants, one for desert plants and one for plants from temperate regions like Australia and South Africa. The tropical house is very warm and humid, so you may want to leave your coats in the cloakroom before you go in.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: To the left of the lake is the woodland walk, a circular path through trees from North America and Asia. It's very peaceful and takes about twenty minutes. And to the right of the lake, between the lake and the east wall, you'll find the visitor centre, with the café, the shop and the toilets.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few words about what goes on behind the scenes. Perhaps the most important part of our work isn't visible at all. In a building behind the glasshouses, we have a seed bank, where seeds of rare species are dried and stored at minus twenty degrees. Stored like this, many seeds can stay alive for decades or even centuries. If a species dies out in the wild, we can grow it again and, in some cases, return it to its natural habitat. That has already happened with a small flowering plant from a Mediterranean island, which we reintroduced in 2015.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: We also run a training programme for gardeners. Each year we take on six trainees, who spend two years working in every part of the garden. Many of them go on to work in other botanical gardens around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A couple of practical points. The garden closes at five, but the glasshouses close half an hour earlier, at half past four, so if you want to see them, don't leave them till last. Please stay on the paths, because some of our plants are very rare, and a few, especially in the medicinal section of the herb garden, are poisonous, so please don't touch or pick anything.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And if you have children with you, they can collect a free activity sheet from the visitor centre. It's a sort of treasure hunt, and anyone who completes it gets a small prize. Okay, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start in the herb garden.

listeningParts.title: A seminar on bilingual children
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two education students, Mei and Joseph, discuss an article on bilingualism with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay, let's get started. Last week I asked you both to read the review article on bilingual children. Mei, what was your overall impression?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I found it really interesting, partly because I grew up speaking Cantonese at home and English at school. The main argument seemed to be that a lot of the fears parents have about bilingualism aren't supported by the research.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Which fears in particular?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: Mainly the idea that learning two languages will confuse children or delay their speech. The article says that bilingual children reach the main milestones, like saying their first words, at about the same age as monolingual children.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Although it did say that if you test them in just one language, bilingual children often seem to know fewer words. That's what worries a lot of parents.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how does the article explain that?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Well, the point is that their vocabulary is split between two languages. A child might know the word for kitchen things in Spanish because that's what they speak at home, and school words in English. If you count the words in both languages together, their total vocabulary is usually the same as, or larger than, a monolingual child's.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. So what's the lesson for teachers?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That you shouldn't assess bilingual children only in the school language, or you might wrongly think they have a language problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, the article also discusses the so-called bilingual advantage. Joseph, what did you make of that section?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: That was the part I found most surprising. I'd always heard that being bilingual makes you smarter, especially at what they call executive function, things like switching between tasks and ignoring distractions. The idea is that bilinguals constantly have to control which language they're using, so they get extra practice.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: But the article said that the evidence is much weaker than people think. Some early studies found big advantages, but they were small studies, and when researchers repeated them with larger groups, the effect often disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: And there's the problem of publication. Apparently, studies that found an advantage were more likely to be published than ones that didn't, which made the effect look stronger than it was.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important general point about research. So where does that leave us?

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: I think the article's conclusion was quite balanced. It said there may be some small cognitive benefits, but the main reasons for bilingualism are cultural and practical. Being able to talk to your grandparents, for instance.

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: I agree. Though the article also said researchers are still arguing about it, so it's probably too early to say there's no advantage at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Which brings us to heritage languages. What did the article say about children of immigrants?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: That many of them gradually lose their parents' language as they grow up, especially once they start school. Often by the third generation, the family language has disappeared completely.

dialogue.speaker: Mei
dialogue.text: That happened to some of my cousins. They can understand Cantonese, but they can't really speak it. And the article said that some parents actually stop using their own language at home because a teacher told them it would help the child's English.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, which is advice the research doesn't support. Okay. For next week, I'd like each of you to find one study on how schools can support heritage languages, and be ready to summarise its method and findings in five minutes. Mei, perhaps you could look at weekend community schools, and Joseph, at bilingual programmes within ordinary schools?

dialogue.speaker: Joseph
dialogue.text: Sure. That sounds really interesting. Should we include our own opinions as well?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Briefly, at the end, but focus on the evidence first.

listeningParts.title: The invention of writing
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory course on the history of communication.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. In this lecture, I'm going to talk about one of the most important inventions in human history: writing. Humans have been speaking for perhaps a hundred thousand years or more, but writing is only around five thousand years old. And unlike speech, which every human community has, writing was invented independently only a few times, perhaps as few as three or four.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The earliest known writing system developed in Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq, about five thousand two hundred years ago. Interestingly, it wasn't created to record stories, poems or laws. The earliest texts are almost all administrative records: lists of goods, such as grain, sheep and beer, and the names of the people who owed or received them. As cities grew and trade expanded, officials needed a reliable way of keeping track of who owed what.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Many researchers believe writing grew out of an older system of small clay tokens, which had been used for thousands of years to count goods. Different shapes represented different things: a cone might stand for a measure of grain, a sphere for a larger measure. These tokens were sometimes sealed inside clay containers, and the shapes were pressed into the outside so that people could see what was inside without breaking the container. Eventually, people realised they could simply make the marks on a flat piece of clay and do without the tokens altogether.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The Mesopotamian script is known as cuneiform, which means wedge-shaped, because the signs were made by pressing a cut reed into soft clay, producing marks shaped like wedges. At first, many signs were pictures of the things they represented, but over time they became more abstract, and scribes began to use signs for their sound rather than their meaning. This was a crucial step, because it meant writing could record any word in the language, including names and grammatical endings.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Clay turned out to be an excellent material for preserving information. Tablets that were baked, either deliberately or accidentally when buildings burned down, became as hard as pottery, and hundreds of thousands have survived. One famous example is the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, where around thirty thousand tablets were preserved when the palace was destroyed by fire in the seventh century BC.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Writing seems to have appeared in Egypt at around the same time as in Mesopotamia, though whether the Egyptians borrowed the idea or developed it independently is still debated. Writing was invented quite separately in China, where the earliest examples, from about three thousand two hundred years ago, are inscriptions on bones used to predict the future. And in Mesoamerica, the Maya developed a sophisticated script that was only fully deciphered in the late twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Early writing systems were extremely complicated. Cuneiform used several hundred signs, and Egyptian hieroglyphs even more, so reading and writing were skills restricted to a small group of professional scribes, who trained for many years. The development that made writing accessible to ordinary people was the alphabet, in which each sign represents a single sound. The first alphabet was created around three thousand eight hundred years ago by people speaking a Semitic language, possibly workers in Egypt who adapted some Egyptian signs. Because it needed only about two dozen letters, it was far easier to learn.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This early alphabet was adopted and adapted by the Phoenicians, who were great traders and spread it around the Mediterranean. The Greeks then made an important change: the Phoenician alphabet had no letters for vowels, so the Greeks added them. The Greek alphabet in turn gave rise to the Latin alphabet, which most European languages use today. Next week, we'll look at the next great revolution in communication: printing.

readingPassages.title: Cracking the code of the Rosetta Stone
paragraphs: For more than fourteen hundred years, no one could read the writing of ancient Egypt. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in the year 394, and after that the knowledge of how the script worked was gradually lost. Later scholars, including Arab writers in the Middle Ages and European scholars of the Renaissance, were fascinated by the mysterious signs carved on temples and monuments, but most assumed that each sign was a symbol expressing a philosophical or religious idea rather than a way of writing the sounds of a language. This assumption, as it turned out, was the main obstacle to decipherment.

The key to the problem was discovered in 1799, when French soldiers who were rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, known in Europe as Rosetta, in the Nile Delta, found a broken slab of dark stone covered with writing. The stone carried the same text, a decree issued by a council of priests in 196 BC, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in demotic, a cursive script used for everyday purposes in Egypt, and in ancient Greek. Since scholars could read Greek, it seemed that the stone might provide the means to understand the other two scripts. When the French were defeated by the British in Egypt, the stone was handed over under the terms of the peace agreement and taken to the British Museum in London, where it remains today.

Copies of the inscriptions were circulated among scholars across Europe, and several made progress. One of the most important early contributions came from Thomas Young, an English scientist and doctor who was also a gifted linguist. Young noticed that some hieroglyphs were enclosed in oval rings, now known as cartouches, and argued correctly that these contained the names of rulers. By comparing the cartouches with the Greek text, he identified the name of the king Ptolemy and worked out the sound values of several signs. However, Young believed that the hieroglyphs were used for sounds only when writing foreign names, such as Ptolemy, which was Greek, and that the rest of the script was symbolic.

The breakthrough came from Jean-François Champollion, a young French scholar who had been obsessed with ancient Egypt since childhood. Unlike Young, Champollion had a deep knowledge of Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, which had survived as the language of the Egyptian Christian church. In 1822, he examined copies of inscriptions from temples in Egypt and found cartouches containing names that were not Greek, but Egyptian, such as that of the pharaoh Ramesses. Using his knowledge of Coptic, he was able to read them. He realised that the hieroglyphic system was a mixture: some signs represented sounds, while others represented whole words or indicated the general category of a word's meaning.

According to a well-known story, when Champollion understood what he had found, he ran to his brother's office, shouted 'I've done it!' and promptly fainted. Whether or not this is true, his announcement in a letter to the French Academy later that year is generally taken as the moment when hieroglyphs were deciphered. Champollion continued to work on the script until his death in 1832, at the age of only forty-one, and published a grammar and dictionary of ancient Egyptian.

The relationship between Young and Champollion has been the subject of debate ever since. Young felt that his contribution had not been properly acknowledged, while Champollion insisted that he had reached his conclusions independently. Most historians now accept that Young made important early discoveries, but that it was Champollion who understood the system as a whole. National rivalry between Britain and France, which had recently been at war, undoubtedly made the dispute more bitter.

The decipherment of hieroglyphs opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history, literature and religion that had been silent for centuries. Thousands of texts, from royal inscriptions to private letters and medical manuals, could now be read. The Rosetta Stone itself has become a symbol of the key that unlocks something previously incomprehensible, and its name has even been borrowed by a well-known language-learning company. In recent years, Egypt has formally requested the return of the stone, arguing that it was removed from the country without the consent of its people.

readingPassages.title: The dance language of honeybees
paragraphs: Among the many ways in which animals communicate, few have attracted as much interest as the dance of the honeybee. When a forager bee discovers a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. Other bees cluster around her, following her movements closely, and soon afterwards many of them leave the hive and fly directly to the food source, even if it is several kilometres away. The dance, it seems, contains precise information about where the food can be found.

This remarkable behaviour was decoded by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for more than fifty years and was awarded a Nobel Prize in 1973 for his work. Von Frisch identified two main types of dance. When food is close to the hive, generally within about fifty metres, bees perform what he called the round dance, running in small circles and frequently changing direction. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction, and they search the area around the hive, using the scent of flowers carried on the dancer's body to help them.

When food is further away, bees perform the waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking her abdomen rapidly from side to side, then circles back to her starting point, first to one side and then the other, so that her path forms a figure of eight. The straight run carries the key information. Its angle relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun: if the bee runs straight upwards, the food is in the same direction as the sun; if she runs at an angle of forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies forty degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of the waggle run indicates distance, with longer runs signalling food that is further away.

Even more impressively, bees take account of the movement of the sun. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a bee that dances for an extended period gradually changes the angle of her waggle run to match. Von Frisch also showed that bees can locate the sun even when it is hidden by clouds, as long as a patch of blue sky is visible, by detecting patterns of polarised light that are invisible to humans.

Not everyone accepted von Frisch's interpretation. In the 1960s, some researchers argued that bees found food not by decoding the dance but simply by following the scent of flowers carried by the dancer. This led to a long and sometimes bitter debate. The question was largely settled in the 2000s, when scientists attached tiny radar transponders to bees that had watched a dance and tracked their flights. Most of the bees flew directly towards the area indicated by the dance, confirming that they were using the information it contained, although they then relied on scent to find the exact flowers.

More recent research has revealed that the dance is not perfectly accurate. The angle of the waggle runs varies slightly each time the bee repeats them, so that the information is somewhat imprecise. Some scientists have suggested that this variation may actually be useful, because it spreads the recruited bees over a wider area of flowers rather than concentrating them on a single spot. Others think it is simply a limitation of the system. Studies have also shown that the relationship between the length of the waggle run and distance differs between populations of bees, suggesting that bees in different regions use slightly different 'dialects'.

The dance is also used for purposes other than food. When a colony becomes too large, part of it leaves the hive with the old queen to establish a new nest. Scout bees search for suitable sites, such as hollow trees, and report back using the waggle dance. Different scouts advertise different sites, and over a period of hours or days, more and more scouts come to support the best site, until a kind of consensus is reached and the whole swarm flies off. The biologist Thomas Seeley has argued that this process is a highly effective form of collective decision-making from which human groups might learn.

readingPassages.title: Does language shape thought?
paragraphs: Does the language we speak affect the way we think? The question is an old one, but it is most closely associated with the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, who argued in the 1930s that speakers of different languages perceive and understand the world in fundamentally different ways. Whorf claimed, for example, that the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammatical forms referring to time, and that Hopi speakers therefore had a completely different conception of time from speakers of European languages. This idea, often called linguistic relativity or the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, became extremely popular, and it remains so outside academic circles.

Within linguistics, however, Whorf's ideas gradually fell out of favour. Later research showed that his claims about the Hopi language were simply wrong: Hopi does in fact have many ways of talking about time. More fundamentally, the dominant approach to language in the second half of the twentieth century, associated with Noam Chomsky, emphasised the features that all human languages have in common rather than their differences. From this perspective, languages were seen as variations on a single underlying system, and the idea that they might shape thought in deep ways seemed implausible. Few linguists, I suspect, regretted the decline of a theory built on such questionable evidence.

In the last thirty years, though, the question has returned, this time investigated with careful experiments rather than anecdotes. Researchers now generally reject the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis, the idea that language determines thought so that some concepts are impossible without the right words. Nobody seriously believes, for instance, that speakers of a language without a word for 'blue' cannot see the colour. But many accept a weaker version: that the habits of a particular language may influence attention, memory and perception in subtle but measurable ways.

One of the most striking lines of research concerns space. In English, we usually describe the location of objects relative to our own bodies: the cup is to the left of the plate. But some languages, such as Guugu Yimithirr, spoken in north-eastern Australia, rarely use words like 'left' and 'right'. Instead, speakers use compass directions, saying that the cup is to the north of the plate, even when talking about objects on a table. To speak like this, people must keep track of their orientation at all times, and studies have found that speakers of such languages are remarkably good at knowing which direction they are facing, even in unfamiliar places or inside buildings.

Colour has also been extensively studied. Russian has two separate basic words for what English speakers call blue: one for lighter shades and one for darker ones. In one experiment, Russian and English speakers were shown three squares of blue and asked which of the bottom two matched the top one. Russian speakers were faster when the two shades came from different categories in Russian, while English speakers showed no such difference. Interestingly, the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they were asked to repeat a series of numbers silently during the task, suggesting that language was actively involved in their judgements.

Grammar may matter too. In languages such as Spanish and German, nouns have grammatical gender, being classified as masculine or feminine. Some studies have reported that speakers describe objects in ways that reflect this gender: for example, that German speakers, for whom the word for 'bridge' is feminine, are more likely to describe bridges as elegant or beautiful, while Spanish speakers, for whom it is masculine, describe them as strong. These findings have been widely reported in the media, but attempts to repeat some of them have failed, and I would treat them with considerable caution.

What should we conclude? It seems clear that language does not imprison thought, as Whorf's more enthusiastic followers suggested. People can think about things they have no words for, and they can learn new languages and new ways of describing the world. Yet the evidence also suggests that the language we speak trains us to pay attention to certain aspects of experience more than others. In this modest sense, Whorf may have been more right than his critics allowed, even if many of his own examples were mistaken.
